newsitem.title: EGYPT: EGYPT SAYS ISRAEL NEEDS PEACE EDUCATION.
newsitem.headline: EGYPT SAYS ISRAEL NEEDS PEACE EDUCATION.

text.p: Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said on Sunday it was Israel rather than the Arabs that needed lessons in peace, just the opposite of what Israeli Prime Minister Benjmanin Netanyahu stated in Washington.
Moussa told reporters that Israel needed to be educated especially on the danger to the Middle East peace process of the Jewish state's settlements policy.
He was responding to comments made last week in Washington during a visit by Netanyahu, who criticised what he said was the lack of "education for peace" in the Arab world.
Netanyahu charged that Arab children still were not being taught to accept Israel as a permanent part of the Middle East landscape.

"If there will be education, then education is needed for those Israelis who support and finance the settlements policy, which is a policy that will destroy the peace process and the atmosphere of peace," Moussa told reporters.
"Only bad can come out of such policy and we cannot expect peaceful relations because it is completely against the spirit of peace," he added.

Moussa said the same idea of peace education could be applied to other areas related to "true and equal peace based on the principle of returning (occupied) land and implementing all that is required by international law".

Egypt, which became the first Arab state to make peace with Israel in 1979, has often criticised Israel's settlements policy and chided Netanyahu for questioning the principle of returning occupied Arab land for peace.
Netanyahu also said in Washington that Israel was "certainly going to develop" existing Jewish settlements in the occupied territories, although it had not decided on new ones.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat warned Israel on Saturday not to "gamble" with Middle East peace by expanding Jewish settlements in occupied Arab lands.
But Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy warned him that he would set back peace moves if his negotiators pressed the issue of settlements at resumed peace talks on Sunday.
Levy and Mahmoud Abbas, the Palestinian chief negotiator also known as Abu Mazen, were due to convene eight joint committees to discuss expanding Palestinian rule.
About 130,000 Jews live in settlements scattered among the more than two million Palestinians of the West Bank and Gaza Strip captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.

The settlements are one of several crucial "final-status" issues to be resolved in talks due to start up again next month. Palestinians fear Israel will speed up expansion of settlements, imposing facts on the ground in advance of future pullbacks.
